(iii) The system did not have a provision for capturing the reason for can-
cellation of the demand bills. 25,626 demand bills were cancelled 
without recording any reasons. 
(iv) Receipt Flag field was used to store the status of payment made against 
a bill (i.e. 0 for non-payment, 1 for payment). In 3,619 cases, though 
there were no payments, the Receipt Flag was “1”. These indicated 
human intervention in the payments of the property tax.
RMC (January 2016) stated that they would check and do the needful for 
demand bills having negative value. For other points, RMC stated that these did 
not have any effect on the property tax system. 
The reply is not tenable as adhoc procedures like deletion of bills without 
assigning reasons rendered the database unreliable and no-one accountable.
4.2.6.6 Non-reliable cheque payments details
Audit observed that details of payment of tax were incomplete and incorrect.
(i) In 328 cases of cheque payment, the cheque number and date were not 
captured.
(ii) Validity of a cheque is generally 90 days from the date of issue. In 140 
cases, cheque dates were more than 90 days prior to the receipt dates. 
These indicated inadequate validation checks in the system.
RMC replied (January 2016) that necessary checks would be added for capturing 
the details of the cheque and adherence to its validity. 
4.2.6.7 Reverse entry of payment on account of dishonoured cheque
RMC facilitated payment of property tax by cash/cheque at the collection 
centres and through online payments. In case of cheque payment, if a cheque 
was returned by the bank due to insufficient balance, the receipt of that payment 
was cancelled/reversed and a fresh demand issued against that property.
Audit observed that a total of 2,262 cheques were dishonoured during  
2010-15. In case of 88 dishonoured cheques amounting to ` 57.63 lakh, the 
receipt entries were not reversed. Audit also noticed that dates of cancellation 
of receipts of 13 bounced cheques amounting to ` 2.97 lakh were even prior to 
the payment dates. 
The management, hence, did not have a dependable system to monitor and take 
appropriate action in case of bounced cheques.
RMC replied (January 2016) that the statement of bounced cheques had been 
submitted to the bank. Only four cheques out of 88 were confirmed by the bank 
and the same would be cancelled after confirmation from the bank. It was further 
added that authoritative controls would be established in the new software for 
monitoring by management and for reverse entry by Accounts Department.
Necessary supervisory checks and alert mechanism may be incorporated to 
ensure timely and corrective action of dishonoured cheques.

106
Audit Report on Local Bodies for the year ended 31 March 2015
4.2.6.8 Refund on account of vacant properties 
The BPMC Act provided for refund of the tax for the properties which had been 
vacant for the number of days such vacancy lasted. It also stipulated that refund 
was not claimable unless notice of vacancy was given in advance. 
Audit observed that no provision was made in the application to handle the entry 
of vacant refunds on account of claims made by the applicants and adjustment 
transactions thereon were manually handled. Adjustment Receipts generated on 
account of vacant refund were also not shown in the ‘properties history’ of the 
properties.
RMC replied (January 2016) that procedure of vacancy refund would be mapped 
in the new developing software with the supportive documents. 
4.2.6.9 Undue discounts to the male owners indicated as female owners
Every year, as motivation, a discount at the rate of 10 per cent was offered for 
making tax payment during April-May and discount of five per cent for making 
payment in June. Additional discount of five per cent was allowed to female 
owners of the property.
Audit observed that in 3,256 assessments, male owners were assigned female 
codes.1,573 such male owners, who made tax payment before July, availed the 
additional discount of five per cent resulting in loss of revenue of ` 2.27 lakh.
RMC attributed these errors (January 2016) to incorrect manual entry. They 
assured that the same would be taken care of in the new software. 
RMC may incorporate adequate input controls and supervisory checks to 
ensure a reliable database.
4.2.6.10 Authorisation checks and Audit trail
In a computerised system, each user should be assigned a role as per the 
responsibilities assigned to him and adequate supervisory checks should exist 
to ensure data security. However, Audit observed that Master data as well as 
transactional data were entered and concurrently authorised by the same user. 
There was no trail of approval of entries by higher authorities;
(i) Out of total 329 users, 21 users were without any designation while 
three users had duplicate USER IDs;
(ii) In 17 assessments, the names of the users who entered the data were 
not captured;
(iii) 62 users who cancelled 1,126 receipts on account of dishonoured 
cheques, were not found in the users table; and
(iv) As per the system, 3,624 property records were deleted during the pe-
riod 2010-15. In 3,209 such records deleted, the identity of the users 
(user id) deleting the record was not captured. 
Thus, the system lacked control over unauthorised operations. In the absence 
of complete audit trails, accountability of the person making such unauthorised 
persons could not be fixed.

107
Chapter-IV : Performance, Information Technology and Compliance Audit of Urban Local Bodies
RMC acknowledged (January 2016) that the system needed updation and checks 
on respective stages for correction/approval by an appropriate authority and that 
they would be incorporated in the new software.
RMC may equip the new software with authorisation controls at various levels 
to check unauthorised operations.
4.2.6.11 Reconciliation of Property Tax with Bank Account
Property Tax was the main source of revenue of the RMC. Weekly/monthly/
yearly income of the Tax was reported to the higher authorities based on the 
Management Information System (MIS) reports of the system. Audit observed 
inadequate reconciliation mechanism and MIS to monitor remittance of property 
tax in the bank.
In absence of bank statements/reconciliation, Audit could not ascertain:
(i) the actual collection of Property Tax 
(ii) actual remittances of cheques 
(iii) actual amount of bounced cheques.
The department did not give specific reply regarding the mechanism to ensure 
actual remittance of property tax in the bank.
RMC may evolve a mechanism for timely reconciliation so to ensure the 
actual remittance of property tax in the bank.
4.2.7 Conclusion 
Property Tax System was developed to reap the benefits of technology to 
improve operational performance, to provide error free and better services. 
However, even after many years of computerization, lack of adequate input 
controls coupled with inadequate monitoring resulted in an incomplete and 
incorrect database. This led to dependency on manual system for fixation of 
rates, deficiencies in generation of demand bills, inability to monitor unpaid tax, 
etc. thereby impacting the collection of revenue. 
4.2.8 Recommendation 
The system may be reviewed with reference to the business rules and current 
requirements. The branches in RMC may be integrated to discontinue the 
manual system of input of data. Appropriate and sufficient input and processing 
controls may be implemented to ensure correct and complete capture of demand 
bills, refunds for vacant properties, deletion of bills, payments and all other data 
related to property tax. These coupled with reduction in manual interventions 
would help in creation of a reliable database. Further, adequate audit trails may 
be incorporated to track the transactions in the system for added security.

dwellers residing nearby. Thus, tardy action on the part of VMC resulted in non-
completion of closure of Vadsar Landfill site scientifically and non-utilisation of 
Government assistance to the tune of ` 1.43 crore
50.

Chapter-IV : Performance, Information Technology and Compliance Audit of Urban Local Bodies
VMC stated (May 2014) that as the site was already covered and did not contain 
any waste, scientific closure was not required, and the dumping of waste was 
strictly restricted. The reply lacks force as VMC had invited tender thrice 
(rejecting though every time) for “Design and Construction of Cover System” 
of Vadsar Landfill site. Further Gujarat Pollution Control Board issued notices 
(from June 2008 to November 2011) to VMC to stop dumping of MSW at the 
Vadsar dumping site after receiving of numbers of complains regarding nuisance 
of air pollution, foul odour and mosquito breeding due to unclosed dumping 
site. The photograph of the site also belies the claim that the site is already 
covered. Audit is of the view that the site may be closed scientifically to comply 
with the environmental standard as per MSW guidelines, restrict the dumping 
of the waste and arrange for alternate residence for slum dwellers to prevent 
occurrence of health related problems to the poor slum dwellers.
The matter was reported to the Government (July 2015). Reply is awaited 
(March 2016).

This Report for the year ended 31 March 2016 has been prepared for submission 
to the Governor of the State of Gujarat.
This Report relates to Audit of receipts and expenditure of the Local Bodies in 
Gujarat conducted under provisions of the Comptroller and Auditor General 
(Duties, Power and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 and read with proviso 
of Gujarat Panchayat Act, 1993, Gujarat Provincial Municipal Corporations 
Act, 1949 and Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963, as amended on 04 April 2011 
which empowers the Comptroller and Auditor General of India to conduct 
Audit of the accounts of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRLs) and Urban Local 
Bodies (ULBs), and submit such Audit Report to the State Government for its 
placement in the State Legislature.
The instances mentioned in this Report are those, which came to notice in the 
course of test audit for the period 2015-16 as well as those, which came to 
notice in earlier years, but could not be reported in the previous Audit Reports; 
instances relating to the period subsequent to 2015-16 have also been included, 
wherever necessary.
The Audit has been conducted in conformity with the Auditing Standards  
(March 2002) issued by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
v

vii
Overview
OVERVIEW
This Report contains four chapters. The first and the third chapters contain an 
overview of the functioning, accountability mechanism and financial reporting 
issues of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) 
respectively. The second chapter contains one Compliance Audit paragraph 
and one individual paragraph on the Audit of financial transactions of PRIs. 
The fourth chapter contains two Performance Audit paragraphs and two 
Compliance Audit paragraphs on ULBs. A synopsis of the findings contained in 
the Performance Audits and Compliance Audits are presented in this overview.
	 1	 An	 overview	of	the	functioning,	accountability	mechanism	and	financial	
reporting issues of Panchayati Raj Institutions
The State Government could devolve only 19 out of 29 functions to the PRIs as 
envisaged in the 11th Schedule of the Constitution. District Planning Committees 
(DPCs) had been constituted in only eight districts. Meetings of DPC were not 
held in these eight districts during 2015-16. The appointment of Lokayukta 
had not been made till December 2016. As on March 2016, 243 Utilisation 
Certificates (UCs) aggregating to ₹ 590.19 crore due in respect of grants 
paid during the period 2001-16 were outstanding. The report of the 3 rd State 
Finance Commission (SFC) submitted in December 2013 was yet to be placed 
before the legislature. The department could implement only nine and seven 
accepted recommendations of first and second SFCs respectively. An unspent 
grant of ₹ 79.45 crore of Thirteenth Finance Commission (ThFC) was lying 
with the PRIs. The State Government has not adopted the Web based software 
(PRIASoft) developed by the Government of India (GoI) for maintenance of 
accounts of PRIs as of date.
(Paragraph 1.1 to 1.10)
 2  Conversion of land from Agricultural to Non-agricultural purposes by 
Panchayati Raj Institutions
The Gujarat Land Revenue Code and Rules enables the Government to monitor 
activities to discourage/indiscriminate conversion of agricultural land for 
non-agricultural purposes. It provided powers to accord necessary permission 
for conversion of land for non-agricultural purposes such as industrial, 
commercial, residential, charitable and temporary use.  Audit was conducted to 
assess whether system for conversion of agricultural land to non-agricultural 
purposes by the Panchayati Raj Institutions was for rightful purpose and in 
accordance with rules and regulations. 
 • Permission for conversion of agricultural land for non-agricultural 
purpose had been granted by the Taluka Development Officers (TDOs) 
instead of District Development Officers (DDOs) and Collectors concerned. 
Permissions had been granted by three TDOs without obtaining approved 
lay-out plan of the Town Planner. 
 • Permission in 270 cases was delayed upto 1,981 days from the stipulated 
date for issuance of permission. 

viii
Audit Report on Local Bodies for the year ended 31 March 2016
 • Permission for conversion of land had been granted without collecting 
conversion tax and measurement fees. Non-levy and Short levy of penalty 
for violation of conditions of permissions were noticed. 
 • Post monitoring of non-agricultural cases was found deficient. 
The above deficiencies need urgent attention of the State Government for 
ascertaining approval of non-agricultural cases for rightful purpose and in 
accordance with the rules and regulations.
(Paragraph 2.1.1 to 2.1.4)
	 3		Idle	 expenditure	 of	 ₹	 13.24	 crore	 on	 underground	 drainage	 project	
besides	depriving	the	targeted	population	of	intended	benefit
Failure to provide connection of drainage line from house to underground 
drainage system resulted in completed underground drainage projects lying 
idle for more than three years despite incurring an expenditure of ₹ 13.24 crore.
(Paragraph 2.2)
 4  An Overview of the Functioning, Accountability Mechanism and Financial 
Reporting issues of Urban Local Bodies
A review of finances of ULBs revealed that Audit of all Municipal Corporations 
(MCs) by Examiner Local Fund Audit (ELFA) was in arrears from 2012-13. 
The MCs and Nagarpalikas (NPs) had not carried out Social Audit of works. 
The State Level Property Tax Board constituted in March 2011 was non-
functional as the assigned functions could not be carried out by the Board. 
UCs for grants aggregating to ₹ 1,040.92 crore paid during the period 2001-16 
were outstanding as of March 2016. The total expenditure against the total 
available funds during the period 2015-16 was 56 per cent. The department 
could implement only 17 and eight accepted recommendations of first and 
second SFCs respectively. An unspent grant amounting to ₹ 126.57 crore of 
ThFC was lying with the NPs and MCs. State’s Municipal Accounts Manual 
has also not been finalized as yet.
(Paragraph 3.1 to 3.13)
 5 Relocation and Rehabilitation of slum dwellers in Ahmedabad Municipal 
Corporation Area
With an aim to improve the quality of life of urban poor, Ahmedabad Municipal 
Corporation (AMC) had prepared (2006) City Development Plan (CDP) for the 
period 2006-12. AMC had also prepared (2012) Slum Free City Plan of Action 
(SFCPoA) for the period 2013-22 based on socio-economic survey (2010) of 
all slum households. AMC identified 572 slums under Slum Free City Plan of 
Action (SFCPoA) to rehabilitate and redevelop through Government funding 
and private developers. The performance audit of “Relocation and Rehabilitation 
of slum dwellers in AMC area” was conducted for the period 2011-16 between 
May and September 2016. Following observations came to light –
 • As against the target of 60,000 Dwelling Units (DUs) under CDP , AMC had 
constructed only 20,112 DUs under Basic Service to Urban Poor (BSUP) 
scheme. Infrastructure development works were not taken up in 149 slums 
identified in the CDP .

ix
Overview
 • Under Slum Free City Plan of Action (SFCPoA), AMC could achieve the 
target of only 10,151 beneficiaries (32 per cent) as of March 2016 against 
the target of 31,578 slum dwellers to be rehabilitated during 2013-15.
 • AMC could recover only ₹ 19.41 crore out of ₹ 119.85 crore recoverable 
from the beneficiaries of 17,915 DUs under BSUP scheme.
 • In BSUP housing project near Saint Mary’s School, Naroda, 192 DUs 
allotted to slum dwellers remained unoccupied since completion of its 
construction (2012) due to the dilapidated conditions of the buildings. 
Similarly, in Ajit Mill Housing Project, Amraiwadi, possession of 40 DUs 
have not been taken by the beneficiaries, out of which 28 DUs are illegally 
occupied.  
 • Social infrastructure such as one Community Hall, one Training Centre, 
four Shops, 10 Anganwadis and 14 Public Health Centres were found non-
functional since completion of their construction (August 2014) under 
BSUP . 
 • Out of 20,112 DUs constructed under BSUP , 2,197 DUs are lying vacant 
since last one to two years as of December 2016.
 • Consent of slum beneficiaries were not obtained for 2,528 DUs under 
construction since September 2014.
 • Under the Regulations for the Rehabilitation and Redevelopment of the 
Slums - 2010 (RRRS-2010), excess Transferrable Development Rights 
valuing ₹ 184.43 crore have been provided to the developers by AMC. 
Permitting the developers to construct low-rise buildings instead of high-
rise buildings resulted in loss of revenue of ₹ 32.62 crore on account of 
vacant area after slum rehabilitation.
 • As provided in RRRS-2010, slum dwellers identified in socio-economic 
survey (2010) were to be considered as eligible beneficiaries. Out of 215 
and 533 DUs allotted in Bavaji na Chapra and Lakhudi Talavadi na 
Chapra projects, only 87 and 306 beneficiaries were covered from the list of  
socio-economic survey respectively.
 • Under In-situ Rehabilitation of Slums - 2013 (ISRS-2013), developers 
of five projects have benefited from lower payment of land premium for 
vacant land due to non-valuation of land with respect to market rate and 
accepting the land premium as quoted by the bidders in their bid. Against 
the average cost of ₹ 4.39 lakh per DU under BSUP , Rajiv Awas Yojana 
and RRRS-2010, the average tender cost approved in six projects for 3,228 
DUs was ₹ 7.69 lakh per DU which resulted in undue financial benefit of  
₹ 106.52 crore to the developers. 
The above deficiencies indicated that the strategies adopted were not effective. 
This is a pointer to the fact that the Government may revisit the policies/
strategies to achieve the intended objective of “slum-free city”.
 (Paragraph 4.1.1 to 4.1.10)

 6 Service Delivery in Urban Local Bodies
With an objective to measure the performance of each ULB, GoI issued (July 
2008) 28 Service Level Benchmarks (SLBs) for four services. The services 
included water supply, sewage, solid waste and storm water management. 
Recommendations of ThFC also provided that each State Government shall 
evolve methods to benchmark the services provided by ULBs. The SLBs issued 
by GoI were operationalised in the State from March 2011. The performance 
audit on “Service Delivery in ULBs” was conducted for the period 2011-16 
between April and October 2016 which revealed some areas of concern relating 
to services delivered by ULBs as highlighted below –
 • NPs test-checked had not prepared the City Development Plan. The SLB 
Cell constituted in November 2011 had not carried out any activity envisaged 
in the Terms of Reference.
 • SLB notification for water supply services indicated that all the MCs had 
achieved the SLBs in respect of per capita supply of water per day, non-
revenue water, water quality and redressal of complaints. All the NPs have 
achieved the SLBs in respect of water quality and redressal of complaints. 
Only 31 NPs in the State could provide prescribed SLB of 135 lpcd of water. 
Efficiency in usage of water and leakages in the distribution system had not 
been ensured in any of the ULBs. Metered water connections had not been 
implemented in any of the ULBs except Surat and Vadodara MCs. None of 
the ULBs in the State could provide water for 24 hours. The supply of water 
ranged between 0.12 hours and nine hours.
 • Discrepancies between actual performance and the performance indicators 
notified in respect of test-checked MCs and NPs were noticed. The actual 
coverage of water connections in Bhavnagar and Vadodara MCs was only 
79 and 90 per cent as against 100 and 98 per cent notified. MCs and NPs have 
been reporting estimated Non-Revenue Water (NRW) instead of measuring 
the actual NRW. No Water Audit had been conducted to assess the actual 
NRW. Out of 13 test-checked NPs, two NPs supplied water on alternate 
days and four NPs supplied water once in three days. Tests prescribed for 
ensuring quality of water was not being carried out by the test-checked MCs 
and NPs. Actual recovery of cost for supply of water varied as compared to 
the recovery of cost notified.
 • Out of 14 Water Supply projects implemented in test-checked ULBs, 
inordinate delay in execution of work was noticed in four projects. Five 
out of ten completed WS projects had not been completely put to use 
by the ULBs due to irregular/non-supply of water from source, faulty 
design and abandoning the work by the agency, etc. Test-checked ULBs 
had not achieved the prescribed SLBs in respect of water supply despite 
implementation of water supply projects.
 • SLB notification for sewage management indicated that all the MCs and 
NPs had achieved the SLBs in respect of coverage of toilets and redressal 
of complaints. The coverage of sewage network in MCs ranged between  

xi
Overview
22 and 98 per cent as against the benchmark of 100 per cent. The coverage 
of sewage network in NPs ranged from zero (96 NPs) to 100 per cent (one 
NP). Sewage treatment facility was available only in five MCs while the 
same was not available with NPs.
 • The actual achievement of coverage of sewage network, cost recovery for 
sewage services and efficiency in cost recovery in respect of test-checked 
NPs varied with reference to achievement notified. 
 • Out of 13 underground drainage projects approved for test-checked ULBs, 
five projects have been completed. Works in respect of seven projects are in 
progress and one project was yet to commence. Delay/non-completion of 
projects had been noticed in test-checked ULBs due to defective drawings, 
change in scope of work, non-construction of pump house, non-availability 
of site, etc. Completed project of Bardoli NP had not been put to use due to 
non-availability of electricity connections. In Unjha NP , the network laid 
was not being fully utilised due to improper laying of network pipelines by 
the agency. 
 • Only two test-checked ULBs had the facility of Sewage Treatment Plants 
(STPs). Instances of disposal of untreated sewage into stream/river/open 
area were noticed.
 • SLB notification for Solid Waste Management services indicated that 
all the MCs and NPs had achieved SLB in household coverage of solid 
waste management services and efficiency in collection of Municipal Solid 
Wastes (MSWs). Segregation of MSWs ranged from two to 18 per cent in 
MCs. Segregation of MSWs was not being done in 155 NPs. Facility of 
processing MSW was not available in three out of eight MCs in the State. 
Only 48 out of 159 NPs had been processing the MSW, however, recovery 
of waste after processing of MSW was notified only in respect of two NPs. 
The facility of scientific disposal of MSW was not available in four out of 
eight MCs and none of the NPs in the State had the facility of scientific 
disposal of MSW.
 • In test-checked MCs and NPs, Audit observed variations in achievement 
notified for Solid Waste Management services as against the actual 
achievement. Segregation of MSW was not being done at Bhavnagar and 
Vadodara MCs as against 17 and two per cent notified. Similarly, variation 
was noticed in test-checked NPs also in respect of achievement notified for 
segregation of MSW. As against 64 and 38 per cent of MSW notified as 
MSW processed by Bhavnagar and Vadodara MCs respectively, the actual 
MSW processed was only 18 and four per cent. Vadodara MC reported 100 
per cent scientific disposal of MSW, however, the actual scientific disposal 
was only 35 per cent of the MSW generated.
 • Vermicompost plants for processing of biodegradable wastes available in 
eight out of 13 test-checked NPs were found non-operational. Sanitary 
Landfill Facilities constructed in January 2013 at a cost of ₹ 46.88 crore 
for covering 36 NPs were not put to use. Resultantly, the NPs resorted to

dumping of MSW in open area and instances of stray animals feeding on 
the wastes were also noticed.
 • Monitoring mechanism was found deficient as SLB Cell constituted had 
not monitored and reviewed the progress of benchmarking process as 
mandated. The notification of achievement of SLB was being done without 
proper assessment.
The above deficiencies need urgent attention of the Government for proper 
delivery of services to the public by the ULBs and to achieve the target of SLBs 
prescribed by GoI.
(Paragraph 4.2.1 to 4.2.13)
 7  Asset Management in selected Nagarpalikas
Audit was undertaken to review the standards of management of 11 important 
assets by the NPs and following deficiencies were noticed.
 • The works to be executed during the year had not been considered while 
preparation of budget estimates instead provision was made on lump-sum 
basis. The NPs had not prepared a five year corporate plan for prioritising 
the development works. 
 • Despite availability of funds, development works had not been commenced 
due to lack of planning. 
 • Ongoing projects had not been completed within the stipulated date of 
completion. 
 • Shops and platforms of shopping complexes and vegetable markets 
respectively constructed by the NPs were found lying idle. The buildings 
were found in dilapidated condition due to non-utilisation/non-auction.
 • NGOs assigned with operation of pay and use toilets had left the work and 
the toilets were found lying idle without proper maintenance.
 • Community halls constructed in Dhoraji and Prantij NPs could not be put 
to use since their construction.

1.1 Introduction
The 73 rd Constitutional amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati 
Raj Institutions (PRIs). It established a system of uniform structure, regular 
elections and continuous funds flow through Finance Commissions. As a follow 
up, the States are required to entrust these bodies with such powers, functions 
and responsibilities so as to enable them to function as Local Self Government 
Institutions (LSGIs). In particular, the PRIs are required to prepare plans and 
implement schemes for economic development and social justice. It also included 
those enumerated in the Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution.
A three-tier1 system of Panchayats was envisaged in the Gujarat Panchayats Act, 
1961. This Act was amended in April 1993 to incorporate the provisions of the 
73rd Constitutional amendment.
The population growth in Gujarat during the last decade (2001-2011) was 19.30

2011, the population of the State was 6.04 crore, of which women comprised

1.2 Organisational set-up of the PRIs
Additional Chief Secretary, Panchayats, Rural Housing and Rural Development 
Department (PRHRDD) exercises administrative control over the PRIs.

and implementation of developmental schemes and administration. The 
PRHRDD exercises administrative control through office of the Development 
Commissioner, Gandhinagar. The President and Vice President of the DPs and

GP is elected directly by the villagers and the Upa-Sarpanch is elected from

the functioning of the DPs, TPs and GPs through Standing Committees having 
elected representatives as members and chairperson. The Presidents in respect of

1.3 Functioning of PRIs
The 73 rd Amendment to the Constitution envisaged transfer of 29 functions 
listed in the 11 th Schedule of the Constitution to the PRIs. Article 243 G of the 
Constitution had empowered the State Legislature to decide and confer powers 
and responsibilities to the PRIs. As per Section 180 (2) of the Gujarat Panchayats 
Act, the State Government may entrust 29 functions to the PRIs to prepare and 
implement schemes3. State Government has, however, devolved (April 1993) 14 
functions fully and five functions partially to PRIs. Ten functions have not yet 
been devolved. This indicated that the spirit of the Constitutional Amendment for 
the PRIs to function as grassroots level LSGIs has not been fulfilled.
1.4 Formation of various Committees
The number of Committees prescribed under the Gujarat Panchayats Act4 is seven5 
for DPs and two6 for both TPs and GPs respectively. In addition, the Panchayats 
may, with the prior approval of the State Government, constitute Committee(s) 
for specific purposes. 
Article 243 ZD of the Constitution of India envisages constitution of District 
Planning Committee (DPC) at district level in every State. DPC consists of such 
number of elected, nominated and permanent invitee members (not less than 15 
and not more than 30) as determined by the Collector of the district. The Minister 
in-charge of the District is the Chairperson of the DPC. The tenure of DPC is five 
years and it is required to meet at least once in three months. 
DPCs are constitutionally responsible to consolidate the plans prepared by Local 
Self Government Institute (LSGIs) in the District. They are also responsible 
for preparing a Draft Development Plan (DDP) of the District as a whole for 
onward transmission to the Government. The DPC is to monitor the quantitative 
and qualitative progress, especially its physical and financial achievements in 
implementation of the approved DDP. The State Government, while preparing 
the State plan, considers the proposal and priority included in the DDPs prepared 
for each District by the DPC. 
DPCs were constituted in only eight districts out of 23 districts; Meetings of DPC 
were not held in these eight districts7 during 2015-16. State could not provide the 
information of remaining 10 districts. This could have factored the aspirations 
and felt needs of the populace.

1.6 Ombudsman
Thirteenth Finance Commission (ThFC) guidelines provided that the State 
Government must appoint “Ombudsman 9” at the State level for LSGIs 10. 
The Ombudsman shall conduct investigations and enquiries in respect of any 
complaints of corruption and mal-administration. Thereafter, it may recommend 
suitable action against the functionaries of both elected members and officials 
concerned in accordance with the provisions of the Act. 
The State Government decided to bring the functionaries of local bodies under 
the jurisdiction of Lok Ayukta. Accordingly, a bill seeking to amend the Gujarat 
Lokayukta Act, 1986 had been passed by the State Legislature on 30 March 2011 
and the Gujarat Lokayukta Ayog Act, 2013 was enacted in September 2014. The 
appointment of Lokayukta is under consideration in General Administrative 
Department of the State.
1.7 Social Audit
The system of Social Audit (SA) was introduced to curb corruption and to promote 
integrity and quality of decision-making in delivery of public services. Social 
auditing is taken up for the purpose of enhancing local governance, particularly 
for strengthening accountability and transparency in LSGIs.
In Gujarat, the PRHRDD had made provision regarding Social Audit of works 
carried out and services provided at Panchayat level in the rules framed for 
“Gram Sabha”(October 2009). Commissioner of Rural Development (CRD) had 
awarded (February 2012) the work of SA of Mahatma Gandhi National Rural 
Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) to “UNNATI 11”. The work was 
initially awarded for a period of two years, which was extended for a further 
period of one year i.e. up to January 2015. The State Government accorded 
(September 2014) the approval of setting-up of independent Social Audit Unit 
(SAU). As against five State Resource Persons (SRPs) at State level and 16 
District Resource Persons (DRPs) at district level, only one SRP and seven DRPs 
respectively have been appointed as of August 2016. 
1.8	Submission	of	Utilisation	Certificates
The Gujarat Financial Rules12 provided that Utilisation Certificates (UCs) for the 
grants should be submitted within 12 months of the closure of the financial year. 
The UCs shall be submitted by the institution or organisation concerned to the 
Head of Department concerned and after verification; these should be forwarded 
to the Accountant General. Audit observed that 243 UCs aggregating to ₹ 590.19 
crore due in respect of grants paid during the period 2001-16 were outstanding 
as on 31 March 2016.

1.9 Internal Audit and Internal Control System of PRI
Internal Audit and Internal Control System in an organisation is meant to ensure 
that they have instituted their own internal audit function. It helps to ensure 
effective management of their own operations and sustain quality of their 
administrative as well as financial performance. It also helps to ensure whether 
the operations are carried out according to the applicable laws and regulations 
and in an economical, efficient and effective manner. A built-in Internal Control 
System and strict adherence to Statutes, Codes and Manuals minimise the risk of 
errors and irregularities. It helps to protect resources against loss due to waste, 
abuse and mismanagement.
The State Government had constituted (1982) an Audit Branch in each DP under 
the direct supervision of an Accounts Officer. The Audit Branch helps all branches 
of the DP in preparation and maintenance of the Accounts, Budget and all other 
required financial statements. All bills of DPs and TPs exceeding ₹ 40,000 are 
being pre-audited by the Audit Branch.

State Government decided (September 2004) to accept the Model Accounting

As per Gujarat Treasury Rules, 2000, the drawing officers are required to furnish 
the Detailed Contingent (DC) Bills in respect of all Abstract Contingent (AC) 
Bills. The DC bills are required to be furnished within three months from the date 
of drawal of AC Bills to Accountant General (A&E). As of May 2016, DC Bills 
in respect of 1,535 AC Bills (2000 to 2016) for an amount of ₹ 41.88 crore were

The State Government may issue instructions to the PRIs for submission of DC 
Bills within the prescribed time limit for timely regularisation of advance drawn 
on AC Bills.

2.1 Conversion of land from Agricultural to Non-agricultural purposes by 
Panchayati Raj Institutions
2.1.1  Introduction
The Gujarat Land Revenue Code1, 1879 (the Code), came into force to enable the 
Government to administer land use in the State. The State Government framed 
(1972) Gujarat Land Revenue Rules, 1972 (GLR Rules) for enforcement of 
the Code. The Code and Rules enables the Government to monitor activities to 
discourage/indiscriminate conversion of agricultural land for non-agricultural 
purposes. It provided powers to accord necessary permission for conversion of 
land for non-agricultural purposes such as industrial, commercial, residential, 
charity and temporary use.
The Additional Chief Secretary (ACS) is the administrative head of Panchayats, 
Rural Housing and Rural Development Department (PRHRDD). He is 
responsible for overall supervision of the PRIs. He is assisted by the District 
Development Officer (DDO) of District Panchayat at the district level and Taluka 
Development Officer (TDO) of Taluka Panchayat at taluka level. The District 
Collector is responsible in the municipal and notified area of the district. The 
DDO is responsible for implementation of policies and rules in rural area under 
the jurisdiction of District Panchayat and the TDO is responsible for areas under 
Taluka Panchayat and Village Panchayat.
An Audit was conducted to assess whether system for conversion of agricultural 
land to non-agricultural purposes by the Panchayati Raj Institutions was for 
rightful purpose and in accordance with rules and regulations. For this purpose, 
Audit test-checked (May 2016 to October 2016) records of seven 2 out of 33 
District Panchayats (DPs) and four Taluka Panchayats (TPs) under each selected 
DPs ( i.e. 28 TPs) in the State. Audit test-checked the records for the period 
2011-16. Audit also conducted joint field visits of 17 non-agricultural lands with 
officials of test-checked DPs and TPs. 
Audit	findings
Audit scrutinised 884 out of 8,845 conversion cases finalised by the test-checked 
DPs and TPs during the period 2011-16. Cases noticed during the regular audit of 
DPs and TPs have also been included in this report.

2.1.2  Approval of conversion of agricultural land to non-agricultural 
2.1.2.1 Permission granted by non-designated official
Sections 65 and 67 of the Gujarat Land Revenue Code provided that the 
authority responsible for grant of permission for conversion of agricultural land 
for non-agricultural purpose shall inspect the sites before and after issuance of

2.1.2.2 Permission granted without approval of the Town Planner
The State Government instructions (March 1982) provided that the applicant 
shall apply directly to the Town Planning Authority for approval of the lay-out 
plan of the proposed land to be converted. The approved lay-out plan was re -
quired to be submitted with the application for conversion of agricultural land to 
non-agricultural purpose.   
In three out of 28 test-checked TDOs, Audit observed in 19 cases 7 that the per -
mission for conversion of agricultural land to non-agricultural purpose had been 
granted without obtaining the lay-out plan approved by the Town Planner. In 
these cases, the applicants had not submitted the approved lay-out plan. The 
TDOs granted the permission without ascertaining the correctness of the plan 
from the Town Planner and granted the permission on the basis of lay-out plan 
prepared by Private Engineer.
With a view to ascertain the correctness of the lay-out plan of the private engineer, 
Audit obtained views of the Town Planner in respect of three cases approved by 
Mundra TP. The Town Planner stated (August 2016) that the permission in these 
three cases could not be granted due to following deficiencies –
•	 Parking space for commercial purpose had not been provided in all the 
cases.
•	 Details of construction work had not been provided by the applicant in the 
lay-out plan in all cases. 
•	 In one case (Samagoga village), the site for construction of commercial 
unit was adjacent to six meter road which is not permissible as per Rule.
This indicated that the TDOs in the above cases had granted permission for 
conversion of agricultural land for non-agricultural purposes without proper 
scrutiny and without following the prescribed procedure leading to undue favour 
to the applicants. 
The TDOs concerned accepted the audit observation and stated (August 2016) 
that due care would be taken in this respect in future.
The State Government may take action to regularize all cases of irregular 
land conversion granted by TDOs instead of DDOs and Collector concerned. 
Strict monitoring mechanism may be established to curb such irregular land 
conversion.

2.1.4 Internal Control Mechanism
2.1.4.1 Maintenance of Land Record
The State Government developed a website ( http://anyror.gujarat.gov.in) to 
facilitate online updation and verification of land records. This enables the user 
of the website to know the type of land use and other information by entering the 
survey number of the land. The authorities responsible for granting permission 
for change in land use are required to send a copy of the non-agricultural order to 
the Mamlatdar of the district. The Mamlatdar16 is responsible for updation of the 
online information. 
Audit scrutinised the details of updation of 69 out of 567 non-agricultural 
cases finalised (2011-16) by Surat DP and six TPs test-checked It revealed that 
information of 22 out of 69 non-agricultural cases 17 had not been updated in the 
website as of September 2016. This defeated the very purpose of development of 
the website for easy access to the public.
As per the provisions of Talati Manual 18 issued (December 2008) by the State 
Government, the Talati-cum-Mantri (TCM) of village panchayat is required to 
maintain non-agricultural control register. Audit observed that the said register 
was not being maintained properly by the TCMs of all test-checked TPs. The 
details of area of land, survey number, area converted for non-agricultural 
purpose, taxes levied and collected, etc. were not being entered in the register. 
The DDOs and TDOs concerned accepted the audit observation and stated (June 
2016) that the register would be maintained in proper form  in future.

The Collector submits quarterly returns to the Revenue department regarding the 
details of permission granted for conversion of land. Audit observed that none of 
the test-checked DPs and TPs had submitted any periodical returns to PRHRDD 
or Revenue Department in this regards during 2011-16. This indicated lack of 
internal control mechanism on the part of State Government in respect of PRIs. 
2.1.5 Conclusion
The Gujarat Land Revenue Code and Rules enables the Government to monitor 
activities to discourage/indiscriminate conversion of agricultural land for non-
agricultural purposes. It provided powers to accord necessary permission for 
conversion of land for non-agricultural purposes such as industrial, commercial, 
residential, charitable and temporary use.  Audit was conducted to assess whether 
system for conversion of agricultural land to non-agricultural purposes by the 
Panchayati Raj Institutions was for rightful purpose and in accordance with rules 
and regulations.

3.1 Introduction
Consequent upon the 74th Constitutional Amendment in 1993, Articles 243 P to 
243 ZG were inserted in the Constitution. These Articles provided constitution 
and composition of municipalities and ward committees, reservation of seats 
for SCs/STs, powers, authority and responsibilities of municipalities, power 
to impose taxes, audit of accounts, elections to the municipalities, constitution 
of district planning committee, etc. This provided that the legislatures could 
endow certain powers and duties to the Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in order to 
enable them to function as LSGIs. It would also enable the ULBs to carry out 
the responsibilities conferred upon them including those listed in the Twelfth 
Schedule of the Constitution.
As per Census 2011, Gujarat ranks sixth after Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil 
Nadu, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh in the tally of most urbanised States. The 
urban population of Gujarat State was 2.57 crore, which constituted 42.55 per 
cent of the total population (6.04 crore) of the State and 2.12 per cent of the total 
population (121.06 crore) of India. In Gujarat, there were 200 ULBs i.e. eight 
Municipal Corporations (MCs), 162 Nagarpalikas (NPs) and 30  Notified 
Areas1 (NAs) as of October 2016. Each MC/NP is divided into a number of 
wards. Wards are determined and notified by the State Government considering 
the population, dwelling pattern, geographical condition and economic status of 
the respective area.

3.3 Functioning of ULBs
3.3.1 Powers and functions
ULBs exercise their powers and functions in accordance with provision of 
Section 87 of the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963. Section 87 of the Gujarat 
Municipalities Act, 1963 provides for various functions to be exercised in the 
sphere of Public Works, Education, Public Health and Sanitation, Development, 
Town planning and Administration. Under Section 63 to 72 of the Bombay 
Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, the State Government had devolved 
various functions and powers to Municipal Corporations.
•	 Devolution of Funds, Functions and Functionaries to Urban Local Bodies
Twelfth Schedule (Article-243 W) of the Constitution of India envisaged that the 
State Government may, by law, endow the ULBs with such powers and authority 
as may be necessary to enable them to function as LSGIs. The State Government 
devolved all the 18 functions envisaged in the Twelfth Schedule to the NPs and 
MCs to enable them to function as LSGIs.

3.4 Formation of various Committees
3.4.1 District Planning Committee 
Article 243 ZD of the Constitution of India envisaged constitution of District 
Planning Committee (DPC) at district level in every State. The tenure of DPC 
is five years and it is required to meet at least once in three months. DPCs are 
constitutionally responsible to consolidate the plans prepared by LSGIs in the 
District. Thereafter, prepare a Draft Development Plan (DDP) for the District 
as a whole for onward transmission to the Government. The DPC is to monitor 
the quantitative and qualitative progress, especially its physical and financial 
achievements in the implementation of the approved DDP. The State Government, 
while preparing the State plan, considers the proposal and priority included in the 
DDPs prepared for each District by the DPC.  
DPCs were constituted in only eight districts out of 23 districts; Meetings of DPC 
were not held in these eight districts2 during 2015-16. State could not provide the 
information of remaining 10 districts. This could have factored the aspirations 
and felt needs of the populace.
3.4.2 Formation of committees in Urban Local Bodies
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation (BPMC) Act, 1949, provided that 
there shall be two mandatory committees in each MC i.e. Standing committee 
and Transport committee. It also provided that the MC may, from time to time, 
appoint out of its own body, special committees which shall conform to any 
instructions that the MC may from time to time give them. As per the information 
provided to Audit, the above mandatory committees have been formed in all MCs 
and additional committees have been formed based on their requirements.
Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963 provided that there shall be two mandatory 
committees in each NP i.e. Executive committee and Pilgrim committee. It also 
provided that the NPs may from time to time constitute other committees to 
exercise the powers and perform the duties of the NP. As per the information 
provided to Audit, the above mandatory committees have been formed in all NPs 
and other committees have been formed based on their requirements.

months, the report shall be sent to the local authority and copies thereof to such 
officers and bodies as the State Government may direct. The ELFA under the

3.12 Internal Audit and Internal Control Systems of ULBs
Internal Audit and Internal Control System is an integral component of ULBs’

that the ULBs’ operations are carried out effectively, economically and 
efficiently. Financial report and operational data are reliable and applicable laws 
and regulations are complied with to achieve objective of providing better civic

had established an independent internal audit wing in the MCs and NPs. The bills 
were passed after pre-audit by the internal auditor.

3.13.3 Recommendations of the State Finance Commission (SFC)
Article 243 I of the Constitution made it mandatory for the State Government 
to constitute a State Finance Commission (SFC). The SFC was to be constituted 
within one year from the enactment of 73 rd Constitutional Amendment and 
thereafter on expiry of every five years. The SFC was responsible to review the 
financial condition of the ULBs and to make recommendations to the Governor 
for devolution of funds. GoI guidelines (June 2005) stipulated that the State 
Government was to act within six months of SFC’s recommendations.
It was, however, noticed 8 that the State Government had neither maintained 
periodicity for constitution of SFCs nor placed report (submitted by the belatedly 
constituted SFC) in the Assembly. This defeated the very purpose of the 
constitution of an SFC.
The State Government had accepted 29 out of 64 recommendations (45 per cent) 
made by the First SFC and 12 out of 42 recommendations (29 per cent) made by 
the Second SFC. The department could implement only 17 and eight accepted 
recommendations of First and Second SFCs respectively (December 2016).
3.13.4 Unspent Grant of Thirteenth Finance Commission
On the recommendation of ThFC, GoI released ₹ 925.76 crore 9 to the State 
Government during the period 2010-15 which was released to the ULBs. Out of 
this, the State Government could utilise only ₹ 799.18 crore 10, leaving unspent 
balance of ₹ 126.57 crore11 as on March 2016.

As per ThFC recommendations, an accounting framework consistent with the

The annual accounts for the year 2014-15 in respect of 158 NPs (except Savli

4.1 Relocation and Rehabilitation of slum dwellers in Ahmedabad Municipal 
Corporation Area
Executive Summary
With an aim to improve the quality of life of urban poor, Ahmedabad Municipal 
Corporation (AMC) had prepared (2006) City Development Plan (CDP) for the 
period 2006-12. AMC had also prepared (2012) Slum Free City Plan of Action 
(SFCPoA) for the period 2013-22 based on socio-economic survey (2010) of 
all slum households. AMC identified 572 slums under SFCPoA to rehabilitate 
and redevelop through Government funding and private developers. The 
performance audit of “Relocation and Rehabilitation of slum dwellers in AMC 
area” was conducted for the period 2011-16 between May and September 2016. 
Following observations came to light –
•	 AMC had constructed only 20,112 Dwelling Units (DUs) against the 
target of 60,000 identified in the CDP and had not taken up the work of 
infrastructure development in 149 slums.
•	 Socio-economic survey conducted in 2010 was found deficient due to 
duplication of names and important information not filled in the forms.
•	 Under SFCPoA, only 572 out of 691 slums were planned for redevelopment. 
AMC could achieve the target of only 10,151 beneficiaries (32 per 
cent) as of March 2016 against the target of 31,578 slum dwellers to be 
rehabilitated during 2013-15.
•	 AMC could recover only ₹ 19.41 crore out of ₹ 119.85 crore recoverable 
from the beneficiaries of 17,915 DUs under Basic Service to Urban Poor 
(BSUP) scheme.
•	 In BSUP housing project near Saint Mary’s School, Naroda, 192 DUs 
allotted to slum dwellers remained unoccupied since completion of its 
construction (2012) due to the dilapidated conditions of the buildings. 
Similarly, in Ajit Mill Housing Project, Amraiwadi, possession of 40 
DUs have not been taken by the beneficiaries, out of which 28 DUs are 
illegally occupied.  

40

•	 Social infrastructure such as one Community Hall, one Training Centre, 
four Shops, 10 Anganwadis and 14 Public Health Centres were found 
non-functional since completion of their construction (August 2014) 
under BSUP . 
•	 Out of 20,112 DUs constructed under BSUP , AMC has  allotted only 
17,915 DUs while remaining 2,197 DUs are lying vacant since last one to 
two years as of December 2016.
•	 Though RAY guidelines envisage obtaining prior consent from slum 
dwellers before commencement of any project, consent of slum 
beneficiaries were not obtained for 2,528 DUs under construction since 
September 2014.
•	 Under the Regulations for the Rehabilitation and Redevelopment of the 
Slums-2010 (RRRS-2010), excess Transferrable Development Rights 
(TDRs) valuing ₹ 184.43 crore have been provided to the developers by 
AMC. This was due to disregarding provisions of Planning Regulation 
for Rehabilitation of slums on Public Land (PRRSPL). Permitting the 
developers to construct low-rise buildings instead of high-rise buildings 
resulted in loss of revenue of ₹ 32.62 crore on account of vacant area 
after slum rehabilitation.
•	 As provided in RRRS-2010, slum dwellers identified in socio-economic 
survey (2010) were to be considered as eligible beneficiaries. Out of 215 
and 533 DUs allotted in Bavaji na Chapra and Lakhudi Talavadi na 
Chapra projects, only 87 and 306 beneficiaries were covered from the list 
of socio-economic survey respectively.
•	 Under In-situ Rehabilitation of Slums-2013 (ISRS-2013), developers 
of five projects have benefited from lower payment of land premium for 
vacant land due to non-valuation of land with respect to market rate and 
accepting the land premium as quoted by the bidders in their bid. Against 
the average cost of ₹ 4.39 lakh per dwelling unit (DU) under Basic 
Services for Urban Poor (BSUP), Rajiv Awas Yojana and RRRS-2010, 
the average tender cost approved in six projects for 3,228 DUs was ₹ 7.69 
lakh per DU which resulted  in  undue  financial benefit  of ₹ 106.52 crore 
to the developers. 
•	 AMC had not made any estimation of affordable houses required in next 
20 years though SFCPoA indicated shortage of 1.27 lakh houses as of 
January 2012.
The above deficiencies indicated that the strategies adopted were not effective. 
This is a pointer to the fact that the Government may revisit the policies/
strategies to achieve the intended objective of “slum-free city”. 
4.1.1 Introduction
The city of Ahmedabad is situated on the eastern bank of the river Sabarmati 
and is now the seventh largest metropolis of our country. Ahmedabad is the hub 
of industrial, trading and commercial activities in Western India and considered

as a model urban centre due to its improved infrastructure and services. Under 
Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (JnNURM), Ahmedabad 
Municipal Corporation (AMC) prepared (2006) seven year plan (2006-2012) “A 
City Development Plan (CDP)” for Ahmedabad. Making Ahmedabad a “slum-
free city” was a goal in the CDP. The Urban Development and Urban Housing 
Department (UD&UHD) had introduced “The Regulations for the Rehabilitation 
and Redevelopment of the Slums – 2010” (RRRS-2010). The RRRS-2010 
provided rehabilitation of slums through private developers which was modified 
by introduction of “In-situ Rehabilitation of Slums - 2013 (ISRS-2013)”. As part 
of slum preventive strategy, UD&UHD announced (July 2013) “Mukhya Mantri 
Gruh Yojana (MMGY)” for providing financial assistance to houses constructed 
for Economically Weaker Sections (EWSs) and Low Income Groups (LIG). AMC 
had also constructed Night Shelters for migrants, homeless people, pavement 
dwellers, etc. to save lives of poor people and preventing them from creating new 
slums.
4.1.2 Organisational set-up 
The Principal Secretary (PS), Urban Development and Urban Housing Department 
(UD&UHD) is the administrative head of the Department. The PS is responsible 
for the overall implementation of housing schemes in the urban areas of the State. 
Mission Director, Affordable Housing Mission (AHM), Gandhinagar is the State 
Level Nodal Agency (SLNA). AHM is responsible for releasing funds received 
from GoI and the State Government under various schemes to the implementing 
agencies.
The Municipal Commissioner (MC) of AMC is responsible for overseeing the 
implementation of these schemes in the AMC areas. The MC is assisted by 
Deputy MCs of Housing Branch, Estate Branch and six Zonal Offices.
4.1.3 Audit Objectives 
The broad objectives of the Performance Audit were to assess whether -
•	 the survey and planning made for relocation/rehabilitation of slum dwellers 
were adequate;
•	 the financial management was efficient and effective; and 
•	 all identified slums were relocated/rehabilitated as per phasing and planning 
made under CDP/SFCPoA through implementation of various schemes/
regulations.
4.1.4 Audit Criteria 
In order to achieve the audit objectives, the following audit criteria were adopted–
•	 City Development Plan (CDP) and Slum Free City Plan of Action 
(SFCPoA);
•	 General Development Control Regulations (GDCR); and 
•	 Regulations, policies, guidelines, instructions/circulars/orders issued by 
the Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation (MoUDPA) 
and the State Government;

and audit criteria were discussed in the entry conference and the inputs of the 
department were obtained. 
The Audit scrutinised the records of six slum rehabilitation schemes implemented

conducted from May to September 2016. Audit also conducted beneficiary

survey work.

UD&UHD to discuss the audit observations. Replies and views of the department 
have been considered in the Report.

4.1.6 Survey and Planning 
4.1.6.1 City Development Plan
JnNURM guidelines envisaged preparation of a “City Development Plan (CDP)” 
by Urban Local Bodies for availing central assistance under BSUP component. 
Accordingly, AMC prepared (2006) CDP for Ahmedabad city for a period from 
2006 to 2012. The main thrust of JnNURM was for integrated development of 
slums through projects for providing shelter , basic services and other related civic 
amenities under BSUP component. To achieve the goal of slum-free city by 2012, 
AMC planned construction of 60,000 Dwelling Units (DUs) for relocation of 
slum dwellers under BSUP. The plan also envisaged infrastructure development 
in 149 slums during 2006-12. 
Audit observed that AMC had constructed (2007-14) only 20,112 DUs against 
the target of 60,000 under CDP. AMC had not taken up work of infrastructure 
development in 149 slums identified under CDP. Deficiencies noticed in the 
implementation of BSUP are discussed in Paragraph 4.1.8.1.

4.1.7.2 Creation of Revolving Fund 
Para 18 of BSUP guidelines provided that 10 per cent of funds received from GoI 
and State Government are required to be ploughed into a Revolving Fund. These 
funds are required to be utilised for operation and maintenance (O&M) of assets 
created under the scheme. Audit observed that the State Government had not 
created a revolving fund of ₹ 25.82 crore as against ₹ 258.23 crore received from 
GoI and the State Government. Draft Project Report prepared by AMC provided 
for formation of a co-operative society with beneficiaries as its members. The 
society is responsible for the O&M of the assets. During joint field visit (22 June 
2016) of Ajit Mill housing project, Audit observed that solid wastes had been 
disposed of by the residents in open plot due to non-establishment of mechanism 
for collection and disposal of wastes from the society (Pictures 1 and 2) . The

assets due to paucity of funds. The beneficiaries had not made the payment of 
their contribution of ₹ 200 per month for O&M and no funds had been provided 
by the State Government for O&M.

4.1.9 Implementation of Regulations for slum rehabilitation through private 
developers
4.1.9.1 Undue favour to the developers by providing excess TDR and relaxation 
in execution of works under RRRS-2010
The State Government constituted (June 2009) a committee for formulation of a 
policy for rehabilitation of slums. Accordingly, the State Government introduced 
(March 2010) “The Regulations for the Rehabilitation and Redevelopment of the 
Slums – 2010” (RRRS-2010). Paragraph 14.3 of RRRS-2010 provided allotment 
of free of cost Dwelling Unit (DU) with basic infrastructure to all eligible slum 
dwellers by the developer. As per Paragraph 12.6.2, the developer would get 
additional Floor Space Index 28 (FSI) for construction of extra DUs/commercial 
units on vacant slum land for sale. UD&UHD amended (May 2012) RRRS-2010 
wherein developers had been provided the option of Transferrable Development 
Right (TDR) for additional FSI29 which could not be utilised on the vacant slum 
plot. The TDR provided could be utilised on any other plot or could be sold to any 
other developer/builder on the basis of proportionate jantri rates 30 of respective 
plots. In case of TDR, the financial benefits to the developers varied, as the jantri 
rates varied among the slum plots selected for in-situ rehabilitation i.e. at the rate 
of ₹ 7,000 to ₹ 36,500 per square metre (sq. mtr.).To rectify this discrepancy in 
RRRS-2010, the State Government introduced (July 2013) a new policy “In-
situ Rehabilitation of Slums 2013 (ISRS-2013)”. Comparison of important 
provisions of RRRS-2010 and ISRS-2013 are shown in Appendix-II. Paragraph 
8.7 of ISRS-2013 (as clarified in Point 8 of General Information in Tender 
Document) provided TDR equal to built-up area used for slum rehabilitation 
multiplied by the ratio of project cost per sq. mtr. and jantri rates. The State 
Government further issued (July 2013) a new planning regulation “Planning 
Regulation for Rehabilitation of slums on Public Land (PRRSPL)”. Paragraph 
7 of the new regulation provided that the decisions taken under RRRS-2010 
stood repealed and TDR would be calculated as per provision in ISRS-2013. In 
case any discrepancy arising on account of applicability of these regulations, the 
decision of the Government should be final. Audit, however, observed that AMC 
followed the provisions of RRRS-2010 and had incorrectly calculated the TDR 
to be provided to the developer. This led to undue benefits to the developers as 
discussed in the succeeding paragraphs. 
•	 Transferrable Development Right 
The UD&UHD had approved (July 2011 to May 2013) 11 projects of AMC 
under RRRS-2010. Out of 11 projects, AMC issued (June 2013 to July 2015) 
commencement letters to the developers of 10 projects. Of these 11 projects, 
eight projects have been completed (January 2014 to November 2015), two 
projects are under progress and one project has not been taken up (September 
2016). All the above 11 projects had been approved for Residential-1 zone (R1).
Audit observed that AMC had not followed the formula provided in ISRS -2013 
for calculating TDR. AMC granted TDR equal to the sum of FSI of gross plot area 
(i.e. 1.8 FSI available in R1 zone as per General Development Control Regulation)

4.1.10.1 Non-preparation of Preventive Plan of Action
RAY guidelines provided preparation of SFCPoA in two parts. Part I for slum 
improvement or redevelopment (curative strategy) and Part II for prevention of 
slums in future (preventive strategy). The preventive strategies would need to 
assess the rate of growth of the city with a 20 year perspective. Based on the 
numbers, specific actions are proposed to be taken to obtain commensurate lands 
or virtual lands and to promote the construction of affordable EWS houses so as 
to stay abreast of the demand.

4.1.10.2 Mukhya Mantri Gruh Yojana
As a part of strategy for prevention of future slums and considering the growing 
need for affordable houses in urban area, State Government announced (July 
2013) Mukhya Mantri Gruh Yojana (MMGY) during the 12 th Five Year Plan. 
Under MMGY , State Government provided subsidy of ₹ 1.50 lakh and ₹ 1.00 
lakh for EWS and LIG houses respectively to the implementing agency. GoI also 
provides central assistance of ₹ 75,000 for EWS house under Affordable Housing 
in Partnership Scheme (AHPS) being a part of RAY . The remaining cost was to 
be borne by the beneficiaries.
GoI and the State Government approved 5,158 EWS houses (Phase I) and 4,293 
EWS houses (Phase II) under AHPS/MMGY . All the houses of Phase I have been 
completed and allotted to the beneficiaries. Construction of houses under Phase 
II was under progress (20 per cent).  Under MMGY , AMC had also taken up 
construction of 4,829 LIG houses (Phase-I) with unit cost of ₹ 9.55 lakh. Audit 
observed that the State Government had approved a project for construction of 
2,866 LIG houses (Phase II) for AMC under MMGY . The State Government had 
released funds of ₹ 14.33 crore in February 2015 to AMC through AHM. AMC 
cancelled the project due to non-availability of beneficiaries subsequently. Audit 
observed that AMC had received 9,654 applications for LIG Phase I project. 
Only 4,829 beneficiaries had been provided LIG houses. People were deprived of 
the benefit of LIG houses when the project was cancelled by AMC.
AMC had not provided reply to audit observation. The Secretary in the exit conference 
(30 December 2016) instructed AMC to provide a detailed reply to Audit.

4.1.10.4 Utilisation of Night Shelters 
Based on the orders (December 2010) of Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, the 
State Government instructed (January 2011) AMC to immediately construct night 
shelters for migrants, homeless people, pavement dwellers, etc. The objective was 
to save lives of poor people and is part of preventive strategy for non-creation of 
future slums. AMC constructed 46 night shelters44 at a cost of ₹ 96.61 lakh with 
unit cost of ₹ 16.60 lakh per night shelter. Audit observed that two night shelters 
were lying unutilised as the policy for its operation and maintenance had not been 
finalised by AMC. Audit further observed that seven night shelters were closed 
between October 2013 and September 2015 and 17 night shelters were not being 
optimally utilized due to their location in the interior area from the main roads 
and lack of proper advertisement in newspapers, media, hoardings, etc. 
The AMC stated (July 2016) that the work of construction of night shelters 
was taken up on war footing under over bridges and plots provided by Town 
Development Officers without proper survey for suitability of locations. It was 
further stated that initially advertisements were given but later on they were 
discontinued. The fact remains that the night shelters remained idle due to lack of 
proper planning and public awareness.

4.2 Service Delivery in Urban Local Bodies
Executive Summary
With an objective to measure the performance of each Urban Local Body (ULB), 
Government of India (GoI) issued (July 2008) 28 Service Level Benchmarks 
(SLBs) for four services. The services included water supply, sewage, solid

4.2.1 Introduction
The urban population of Gujarat State was 2.57 crore as per census 2011, which 
constituted 42.55 per cent of the total population (6.04 crore) of the State. This 
constituted 2.12 per cent of the total population of India (121.06 crore). The Urban 
Local Bodies (ULBs) in the State consisted of  eight Municipal Corporations 
(MCs), 162 Nagarpalikas (NPs) and 31 Notified Areas. 

65
Chapter-IV : Performance and Compliance Audits of Urban Local Bodies
The 74th Constitutional amendment in 1993 endowed responsibilities 45 listed in 
the Twelfth Schedule to the ULBs to function as institutions of self-Government. 
Government of India (GoI) made huge investments over the years through 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes and by devolution of direct funds as per the 
recommendations of various Finance Commissions. 
Benchmarking is well recognized as an important mechanism for introducing 
accountability in service delivery. It involves measuring and monitoring of service 
provider’s performance on a systematic and continuous basis. Recognizing 
its importance, Ministry of Urban Development (MoUD), GoI had launched 
the Service Level Benchmarking (SLB) initiative in July 2008 covering four 
services namely water supply, sanitation, solid waste management and storm 
water drainage (Appendix-VII). Thirteenth Finance Commission (ThFC) in 
its recommendation for the period of 2010-15 mandated that State Government 
should put in place standards for delivery of essential services by Local Bodies 
among the fulfilment of other conditions linked to the access of the performance 
grants. 
4.2.2 Organisational set-up
The Additional Chief Secretary (ACS), Urban Development and Urban Housing 
Department (UD&UHD) is the administrative head of the department. Director 
of Municipalities (DoM) exercises administrative supervision of the NPs. The 
Gujarat Municipal Finance Board (GMFB) is responsible for distributing funds 
to MCs and NPs. 
Gujarat Urban Development Mission (GUDM) is the State Level Nodal 
Agency (SLNA) for implementation of Centrally Sponsored Schemes 
(CSS) and State Sponsored Schemes (SSS). GUDM accorded administrative 
approval and technical sanctions for projects submitted by the ULBs. 
Water Supply Schemes (WSSs) are implemented either by Gujarat Urban 
Development Company (GUDC), Gujarat Water Supply and Sewerage Board 
(GWSSB) or the concerned ULBs. Underground Drainage Schemes (UDSs) 
are implemented by GUDC or GWSSB and Solid Waste Management (SWM) 
are implemented by GUDC.
4.2.3 Audit Objectives
The objectives of the Performance Audit were to ascertain whether – 
•	 proper planning was done to put in place standards of service delivery of all 
essential services to be provided by ULBs;
•	 ULBs were able to provide the basic urban services; and 
•	 an effective mechanism was in place to make the service level benchmarking 
operational as well as monitor and evaluate performance on provision of 
basic urban services.
 45 Responsibilities under Twelfth Schedule included urban planning (including town planning), regulation of land-use 
and construction of buildings, planning for economic and social development, roads and bridges, water supply for 
domestic, industrial and commercial purposes, public health, sanitation, conservancy and solid waste management, 
fire services, provision of urban amenities and facilities such as parks, gardens, playgrounds, etc.

The Performance Audit commenced with an ‘entry conference with the UD&UHD. 
The Audit objectives, scope and methodology of Audit were discussed. The audit

and notification of SLBs, and implementation of WSS, UDS and SWM projects. 
Achievements of SLBs in respect of three out of four services have been covered 
in Audit i.e. Water Supply, Sewage Management and Solid Waste Management 
(SWM). Storm Water Management was not covered as Gujarat is a rain deficit 
State and the work related to Storm Water Management had not been taken up 
on large scale in the State. Records maintained in the offices of the  UD&UHD, 
GUDM, GMFB, GUDC, two out of eight MCs 46 and 13 out of 56 “A” and “B”

of MCs and NPs was done with population as measure of size. Joint field visit 48

delivery of services to the populace.
An exit conference was held (13 January 2017) with the Secretary, UD&UHD and 
Additional Chief Executive Officer of GUDM to discuss the audit observations. 
Replies and views of the department have been incorporated in the Report.
Audit	findings
Audit findings are based on the scrutiny of records related to the works done 
and measures taken by the ULBs to improve their performance against the SLBs

The DoM stated (December 2016) that though CDP was not prepared, the actual

4.2.6.2 Notification of Service Level Benchmarks
The Thirteenth Finance Commission (ThFC) grants are divided into two 
components – General Basic Grant (GBG) and General Performance Grant 
(GPG). GPG can be accessed only on complying with the conditions stipulated 
in the ThFC Report. One of the conditions of ThFC envisaged that the State 
Government shall notify targets and achievement for SLBs each year for each 
ULB. 
Hand Book on Service Delivery issued by MoUD prescribed methods of 
measurement and calculation of benchmarks. The reliability of these benchmarks 
are fixed on the basis of methods adopted in measuring the benchmarks. It also 
envisaged that the State Governments and their nodal agencies need to evaluate 
periodically the SLBs. The results of evaluation shall be considered as an 
input for decision making relating to policy, allocation of resource, incentives 
and penalties, channelizing technical and manpower support and regulatory 
considerations among others. GUDM was the nodal agency to operationalise the 
SLB framework in the State. 
Audit observed that neither the GUDM nor the test-checked ULBs had been 
maintaining any records regarding methods adopted for assessing the achievement 
and fixing of targets for SLBs. No system existed in respect of regular collection 
of data from ULBs by GUDM. 
Audit observed that State Government had been notifying targets and 
achievements of SLBs from the year 2011-12 based on the work done by Centre 
for Environment Planning and Technology (CEPT) University. CEPT University 
have been conducting research project named “Performance Assessment System 
(PAS)” on water supply and sanitation in ULBs of Gujarat and Maharashtra 
States. The project is being funded by Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. Based 
on the information collected from ULBs for their project, CEPT developed a 
website with online tools/modules for fixing targets and calculating achievement. 
The said database of the CEPT was being utilised by the State Government for 
notifying the achievement of SLBs.

68
Audit Report on Local Bodies for the year ended 31 March 2016
This indicated that achievement and targets of SLBs were being notified without 
proper measurement and without analysing the actual facts at ULB level by the 
Nodal Agency (GUDM) as discussed in Paragraph 4.2.7, 4.2.9 and 4.2.11. It is 
apparent that the notifications are being issued only for meeting the conditions of 
ThFC for obtaining GPG.
The Secretary in the exit meeting stated (January 2017) that the work of notification 
of benchmarks was done regularly with the assistance of CEPT University and 
Urban Management Centre (UMC). The fact remained that the State Government 
failed to perform their work in this respect and the objectives of operationalising 
the SLBs in the State were not achieved.
4.2.6.3 Functioning of Service Level Benchmarks Cell
Ministry of Urban Development, GoI issued (October 2010) instructions to the 
State Government to constitute a SLB Cell at the State level. Accordingly, State 
Government constituted (November 2011) an SLB Cell with Principal Secretary, 
UD&UHD as Chairperson and Additional Chief Executive Officer, GUDM as 
member secretary. The Cell was required to meet once in three months to review 
and monitor the progress of benchmarking process in ULBs.
The UD&UHD issued (December 2012) Terms of Reference (ToR) of the Cell. 
The ToR provided that the Cell shall collect from time to time, the information 
regarding achievement of SLBs by each ULB. The Cell shall assist the ULBs 
in preparing Information System Improvement Plan (ISIP) and Performance 
Improvement Plan (PIP). The ToR also provided that the Cell shall publish 
annual SLB data book for all the ULBs in the State by 31 st July every year and 
prepare quarterly reports of activities 49. As per ToR, the Cell shall meet once in 
every month.
Audit observed that the Cell had not carried out any activity envisaged in the ToR. 
Against four meetings required to be held before December 2012 and monthly 
meeting thereafter, only one meeting of the Cell had been held till December 
2016.
GUDM stated (November 2016)  that though only one meeting was held, 
UD&UHD had been monitoring the works under SLB on regular basis. The reply 
of GUDM is not acceptable as the Cell was responsible for operationalising, 
reviewing and monitoring the SLB framework in the State, which was not being 
done as it remained non-functional since its constitution.

Hand book on SLB prescribed nine benchmarks to measure the performance of 
water supply (WS) services –

•	 Continuity of water supply  – 24 hours supply of pressurised water per 
day;
•	 Extent of Non-Revenue Water  - the revenue that could not be realised 
from water which has been lost through leakages, thefts, etc. The maximum

number of complaints received to be redressed within 24 hours; and
•	 Efficiency	in	recovery	of	water	supply	charges	-	It is the revenue collected 
in the current year against the total demand of operating revenues.

4.2.7.1 Discrepancy in performance of SLB notified for water supply
The benchmarks notified in respect of test-checked MCs and NPs were scrutinised

which are discussed below –

respectively. The percentage of water connections in test-checked NPs 
ranged between 64 (Gandhidham) and 98 (Amreli) as per notification. The 
actual percentage of water connections ranged between 50 (Bardoli) and 95 
(Anjar and Modasa).

In test-checked ULBs, 14 WS projects50 had been implemented under UIDSSMT

4.2.8.2 Utilisation of completed water supply projects
In five out of ten completed WS projects, it was observed that though the projects 
have been operationalised, three 53 ULBs could not achieve the prescribed SLB 
of supplying 135 lpcd potable water. Remaining five completed WS projects had 
not been put to use by the ULBs as discussed in the succeeding paragraph -
(i) Dholka NP supplied 4.65 MLD water through tube wells to the city upto 
2010. The NP proposed a water supply project to the State Government indicating 
in the Detailed Project Report (DPR) that the ground water was not fit for use 
due to excessive drawl of ground water over the years. Accordingly, the State 
Government approved (March 2010) Narmada Canal based water supply project 
at a cost of ₹ 9.77 crore under SJMMSVY . The project envisaged supply of 16.21 
MLD water considering the expected demand by the year 2041. The ULB started 
the work in October 2010 and completed the same in January 2015 at the cost of ₹ 
9.77 crore. Audit observed that the NP was still supplying underground water and 
had been incurring recurring expenditure of ₹ 1.50 crore per annum on electricity 
charges for drawing ground water. 
The Chief Officer stated (June 2016) that the water from tube wells was being 
utilised due to irregular supply of water from Narmada Canal. The Secretary in 
the exit meeting (January 2017) stated that the NPs showed unwillingness to 
draw water from Narmada as they have to pay the charges raised by the Irrigation 
Department. This indicated that despite spending an amount of ₹ 9.77 crore 
on the canal based water supply project, NP continued to exploit ground water 
which was not fit for use due to excessive drawl of water as stated in the DPR. 
Resultantly, the infrastructure created was not being fully utilised and the very 
purpose of supplying treated water and further depletion of ground water were 
defeated.
(ii) Mahuva NP had been supplying 45 lpcd of water to the town through tube 
wells. The State Government approved (November 2009) a WS project at a cost 
of ₹ 17.66 crore under SJMMSVY with source of water from Narmada Canal. 
The project envisaged supply of 26.48 MLD water considering the expected 
demand by the year 2038. The project work involved laying of distribution 
pipelines, construction of storage structures, pump houses and Water Treatment 
Plant (WTP) and installation of pumping machines. GWSSB started the work in 
March 2012 and completed the same in March 2013 at a cost of ₹ 17.70 crore.
Audit observed that the NP had not included in the DPR, the cost of pumping 
machines required for pumping of raw water and its treatment. It was contemplated 
by the NP that the old and existing pumping machines would be utilised for this 
purpose. Later, the NP realised that the existing machines were not sufficient 
to pump raw water into the WTP and treated water to distribution network. 
Resultantly, the raw water drawn had not been fully treated. 
During joint field visit (24 May 2016), it was observed that the treated and raw 
water was being first filled in a sump and then supplied to the city. This defeated the 
very purpose of supplying clean water to the public. The supply of water through
